read.title: Moving graphs without redrawing them
text: Once you know the graph of a basic function, you can sketch many related functions by transforming it. Start with y = x², a U-shaped parabola with its vertex at the origin.

Adding a constant outside the function changes every output. The graph of x² + 3 is the same parabola lifted 3 units. Multiplying outside stretches outputs: 2x² rises twice as fast. A minus sign outside, −x², flips the parabola upside down across the x-axis.

Changes inside the function act on inputs, and they behave in the opposite way from what the symbol suggests. In (x − 2)², the output that x² gave at x = 0 now appears at x = 2, so the graph moves right, not left. Likewise f(2x) reaches each output at half the input, so the graph compresses horizontally toward the y-axis.

Combining these lets you read a formula like y = −(x − 2)² + 5 at a glance: shift right 2, flip, then shift up 5. The vertex lands at (2, 5) and the parabola opens downward. Calculus uses this skill constantly, because recognizing the shape of a function tells you where to expect its maximum, minimum, and steepest parts.

q.q: Why does (x − 2)² sit to the right of x²?
o: Each output now occurs at an input 2 larger
